**The Weight of a Name**

The first time I saw the name *Kaelani* carved into the bark of a tree, I didn’t recognize it. Not at first. The letters were jagged, uneven, as if someone had pressed them into the wood with their fingers rather than a knife. But when I traced the curves of the *a* and the sharp angle of the *K*, something in my chest tightened. It wasn’t just the shape of the letters—it was the way they *felt*. Like a secret.

I was twelve when I found it. My father had taken me to the old growth forest behind our house, the kind where the trees were so tall they swallowed the sky. He’d been teaching me how to identify edible mushrooms—*morels*, *chanterelles*—but I’d been more interested in the way the light filtered through the canopy, turning the forest floor into a mosaic of gold and green. Then I saw it: a name, half-buried in the bark, as if someone had tried to hide it.

I didn’t ask where it came from. Not then. My father was quiet about a lot of things, especially the years before I was born. But later, when I was older, I’d learn that the forest had been his refuge. That he’d carved names into trees when he was a boy, names of people he loved, or maybe names of people he’d lost. Some were his own, others belonged to strangers he’d met in passing. A girl named *Lila* with freckles like scattered stars. A boy named *Rafael* who’d taught him how to swim. *Kaelani* was different. It wasn’t a nickname or a first name—it was a place. A word that meant something to him, even if he never spoke it aloud.

I didn’t tell him about the name that day. I didn’t tell him about any of it. But I started coming back. Every weekend, when the house was too quiet, when the weight of my mother’s silence pressed down on me like a physical thing, I’d slip out the back door and into the trees. I’d find the tree with the name, run my fingers over the letters, and pretend, just for a moment, that it was mine.

Years passed. The bark grew thicker, the letters faded. But I kept coming back. Because names, I learned, are more than just sounds. They’re the way people try to hold onto each other when the world is trying to let go.

One autumn, when I was seventeen, I found a new name. It was smaller, more recent, carved into the same tree. *Eli*, it said. Just one word, but it was there, fresh and sharp. I didn’t recognize it. I didn’t know anyone named Eli. But I knew, without asking, that it was someone important to my father. Someone he’d been keeping secret.

That night, I sat on the porch and waited. The air was cool, the kind of cool that made your breath visible. I heard the crunch of leaves underfoot before I saw him. My father stood at the edge of the trees, his hands in his pockets, his face half-lit by the porch light.

“You found it,” he said.

I didn’t answer. I just looked at the name. *Eli*.

“He’s not here anymore,” my father said softly. “But I thought… I thought you should know.”

I didn’t ask who *he* was. I didn’t ask why my father had been writing names in trees like they were prayers. I just nodded, because some things don’t need words.

The next morning, I carved my own name into the bark. *Mira*, I wrote. Not because I thought it was special, but because it was mine. And maybe, just maybe, if I left it there, someone else would find it one day and know they weren’t alone.

---

**The Last Letter**

The letter arrived on a Tuesday. It was thick, the kind of envelope that made your fingers ache just from holding it. My mother had been gone for three years, but letters still came sometimes. Most were bills, or condolences from people who didn’t know what to say. This one was different. The return address was in a city I didn’t recognize—*Port-au-Prince*—and the handwriting was slanted, confident, like someone who knew they were being remembered.

I sat on the edge of my bed and tore it open.

*Dearest Mira,*

*I know it’s been a long time. Longer than I ever thought possible. But I had to write. Not because I expected an answer, but because I needed you to know—*

I stopped reading. The words blurred. My hands trembled. I hadn’t heard my mother’s voice in so long that it took a moment to realize it was still there, whispering through the paper.

*I’m sorry.*

The letter went on for pages. She wrote about the years she’d spent abroad, about the life she’d built without me, about the choices she’d made that had torn us apart. She didn’t excuse herself. She didn’t ask for forgiveness. She just said it, plain and simple: *I’m sorry.*

I read it three times before I could bring myself to fold it back up. Then I tucked it into my pocket and walked to the old oak tree in the backyard. The bark was rough under my fingers, but I found the name I’d carved years ago—*Mira*—and pressed the letter against it. Maybe, I thought, if I left it there, the tree would remember her too.

---

**The Thing About Names**

People ask me sometimes why I collect names. Why I write them down in notebooks, why I carve them into wood, why I memorize them like they’re spells. I tell them it’s because names are the first things we give to the people we love. They’re the way we say, *This is who you are. This is who I see.*

But the truth is, names are also the last things we keep when everything else is gone. They’re the way we hold onto each other when the world tries to take us apart.

So I write them down. I carve them into trees. I say them out loud, even when no one’s listening.

Because names are promises. And promises, no matter how broken, are still promises.
